Need to search first.I've finished, but the research didn't get as far as planned. My search tool hit its usage limit after the first round of searches, so I couldn't open any pages in full. Everything below comes from the page text returned in those search results. That text was often only part of a page, so some verses are covered thinly. I found nothing from the Lutheran, Orthodox or catholic.com sites, no netbible.org translator notes (the NET page returned the wrong chapter), and nothing on prosperity or word-of-faith readings of this psalm. Those gaps are noted at the end rather than filled in.

---

## Background and title
- Enduring Word (Guzik) thinks David wrote the psalm around the time all the tribes accepted him as king. It quotes George Horne that vv. 2 and 10 point to a time after David came to the throne, while v. 5 shows enemies were still left. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Gill says David wrote it for himself as king, not as a prophecy of the return from Babylon (Theodoret's view). He places it between or after David's wins over the Philistines. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/144.htm
- Ellicott calls vv. 1–11 a patchwork drawn mostly from Psalm 18. He thinks vv. 12–15 are a piece of an older song, perhaps a harvest song, that doesn't connect to what comes before. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- Spurgeon disagrees strongly. He sees the psalm as one complete poem and says splitting it would be "literary Vandalism." He thinks it is clearly by David. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps144.php
- Constable calls it a royal psalm asking for victory in war, a "mosaic" built mostly from Psalm 18. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-144.html

## Verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- Guzik says David gave God, not himself, the credit for his fighting skill. The verb "trains" is in the present tense, so the training goes on, whether with real weapons or spiritual ones such as the "sword of the Spirit." He quotes Trapp: David's hands knew the shepherd's crook and the harp before God fitted them for war. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Spurgeon blesses God for skill as well as strength, since untrained strength is dangerous. He argues that if God helps with something as unspiritual as fighting, he will surely help with preaching the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/144-1.htm
- Gill notes that the Greek and Latin translations read "my God" for "my Rock." God took David from shepherd to general. Gill also applies the verse to God arming believers for spiritual warfare. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/144.htm
- Barnes thinks "fingers" refers to using the bow: placing the arrow and drawing the string. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-144.html
- Calvin prefers "strength" to "rock." David had a warlike spirit but was not born a warrior and needed God to change him. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_144:1-2
- Constable cites the NET Bible note that Egyptian carvings show gods teaching the king to shoot a bow. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-144.html
- Two writers in the Pulpit Commentary's sermon section disagree about war:
  - S. Conway says psalms like this are far from the spirit of Christ and are best read as being about spiritual conflict.
  - R. Tuck argues that God has sometimes approved even aggressive wars, but judges nations that use their trained power for selfish ends.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/144.htm
- The Church Pulpit Commentary refuses to separate Israel's real wars from spiritual ones. It applies the verse to fighting fleshly desires, worldly pressure and the devil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/psalms-144.html

**v. 2:**
- Guzik notes that the list of names for God starts with *hesed*, God's loyal covenant love. "Subdues my people under me" probably means the tribes accepting David as king (2 Samuel 5), or possibly the fighting men who gathered around him earlier (1 Samuel 22). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Ellicott says "my goodness" is short for "God of my grace." Some manuscripts read "peoples," as Psalm 18 does. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says "my goodness" appears nowhere else in Scripture, a sign of an original author rather than a copyist. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-144.html
- Calvin says piling up titles for God is not wasted words; it strengthens faith. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_144:1-2
- Wesley: God made the people's hearts willing to obey David as king. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-144.html
- Clarke (Methodist) suggests it may refer to the peace after Absalom's rebellion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/144-2.html
- Matthew Henry: ruling well is a harder and nobler skill than fighting, and God's providence keeps people loyal to their rulers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_144.cfm
- In his shorter commentary, Henry sees Israel's loyalty to David as a picture of souls being brought under Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/144.htm
- Spurgeon notes how often David says "my." Peace at home deserves as much thanks as victory in war, and church leaders also depend on God for any influence they have. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps144.php

**v. 3:**
- Guzik: having praised God's greatness, David is amazed that God cares about humans at all. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Gill: man is dust and sinful, yet God knows him through providence and grace. Gill links the verse to Psalm 8:4 and its application to Christ in Hebrews 2:6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/144.htm
- Spurgeon: "son of man" stresses man's weakness even more. That God thinks so highly of man in redemption "can be believed, but it cannot be explained." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps144.cfm
- A writer quoted in Spurgeon's notes says it is fitting that, right after mentioning his own power over others (v. 2), David humbles himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps144.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: remembering how small and unworthy we are makes God's goodness look greater. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-144.html
- Augustine (Catholic, Church Father): God values man so highly that he gave his Son's blood for him (Romans 8:32). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801144.htm

**v. 4:**
- Guzik: David had seen so much death that he knew how brief life is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Ellicott: the thought might be a warrior's humility, a lament over fallen comrades, or both. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- Barnes: a shadow has no substance and keeps moving until it disappears; so does a human life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-144.html
- Gill compares the "breath" to the vapour of James 4:14. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/144-4.html
- Bible.org: the verse stresses human limits, and by implication God's eternity. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-144
- Augustine: "vanity" here means passing time, compared with the God who says "I Am." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801144.htm

**vv. 5–6:**
- Guzik: the language recalls God's appearance at Sinai (Exodus 19) and conveys awe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Wesley: a poetic picture of God coming to punish his enemies; the mountains smoke as Sinai did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-144.html
- Ellicott says the wording comes from Psalm 18 with some original touches. "Flash forth lightning" uses a verb found only here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- Gill says God's "coming down" must be squared with his being everywhere. He reports that some read it as a prayer for Christ's incarnation, and he takes the "mountains" as kings and kingdoms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/144.htm
- Spurgeon: God most fully "came down" at Bethlehem. Once we accept that God cares about us at all, it is a small step to expect him to use his power for us. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps144.php
- Augustine takes the heavens being bowed as the apostles humbling themselves, the "mountains" as proud people who smoke when God touches them, and the lightning as miracles. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801144.htm

**vv. 7–8:**
- Pulpit Commentary:
  - "Deep waters" is a common image for serious danger.
  - The foreigners are "sons of strangers," that is, foreign enemies.
  - "Falsehood" may hint at a pretended surrender.
  - The right hand was raised when swearing an oath, so a "deceitful right hand" means a broken oath.
  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-144.html
- Ellicott also links the right hand to oath-taking. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- Guzik says "foreigners" is not about nationality; these people showed by their actions that they were strangers to God's people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Spurgeon: they were either outsiders such as Philistines and Edomites, or treacherous Israelites who were strangers at heart. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps144.php
- Wesley gives the same two options. "Speak falsehood" means empty boasts and threats that will come to nothing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-144.html
- Gill sees the "great waters" as afflictions or many enemies, and also applies them to Christ's sufferings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/144.htm
- Augustine: the waters are unbelieving peoples, whether attacking from outside or plotting within. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801144.htm

**v. 9:**
- Guzik: new deliverances call for a new song. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Ellicott: this is the only use of the name *Elohim* (God) in the last two books of the Psalms, apart from Psalm 108. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- Gill: new mercies call for new songs. He also reads it as a song for the New Testament age of new covenant and redemption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/144.htm
- Augustine: the new song belongs to grace and the New Testament. The "ten strings" are the Ten Commandments, because love fulfils the law. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801144.htm
- For instrumental music, see Part 2.

**v. 10:**
- Spurgeon: kings face special danger, so a king who survives should give God the glory. David calls himself God's "servant," the highest title he wanted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/144.htm
- Gill: kings are preserved by God's providence, not by their bodyguards. He also applies the verse to Christ, the Son of David, delivered from death in the resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/144.htm
- Matthew Henry: escaping the sword means little without deliverance from sin and the coming judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/144.htm
- Augustine contrasts the "sword of ill intent" (lying tongues) with the good sword of Matthew 10:34, the word of God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801144.htm

**v. 11:**
- Gill: the repetition of vv. 7–8 shows how urgently David prayed and how much danger he was in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/144.htm
- Barnes: thinking of the answer, and of the praise it would bring, interrupted the prayer, which now picks up again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-144.html
- Constable calls v. 11 a refrain. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-144.html

**v. 12:** Interpreters disagree about who is being described here. See Part 3.
- Guzik: David asks God to bless his people's everyday life, and the list reflects the concerns of farming families. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Wesley: David asks this for his people's sake, not just his own. Sons are a nation's strength and hope; daughters as "cornerstones" means strong and beautiful. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-144.html
- Ellicott says the word "plants" means young, vigorous, newly planted trees. He rejects the idea that the "corner pillars" are carved statues of women. He reads the picture as hewn stone corners, an image of unassailable virtue. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- S. Conway (Pulpit sermon section) sees in the plant and the pillar rootedness, visible character, strength and beauty. He notes the psalm honours daughters as much as sons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/144.htm

**v. 13:**
- Barnes: the Hebrew means "every kind" of produce; flocks were much of Palestine's wealth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/144-13.htm
- Another commentary on the same page says the word for "kind" is Aramaic, which suggests a late date, and that "streets" should be "fields." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/144-13.htm
- Ellicott also renders "fields" (open pastures). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- Matthew Henry (shorter commentary, quoted on the same page): plenty is good if it makes us thankful, generous and charitable to the poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/144-13.htm

**v. 14:** Ellicott calls this verse "full of obscurities."
- Ellicott thinks the Hebrew can't easily mean "oxen bearing loads." He prefers "our princes firmly established." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- Barnes says the word means "laden," most likely with young: cattle multiplying. He takes "no breaking in or going out" as livestock and property kept safe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/144-14.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: oxen heavily laden with harvest, no breach in the walls, no one carried into captivity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/144-14.htm
- Wesley: no enemy breaking through the walls, and no going out, either to fight or into captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-144.html
- Gill lists several readings, including one that refers it to miscarriage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/144-14.htm
- Spurgeon: no raiders, no forced emigration, no unrest in the streets. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps144.php
- Guzik quotes Clarke: a land so well policed that it has no robbers or raiders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/

**v. 15:**
- Guzik: real happiness belongs to people whose God is the LORD, and this holds for Christians under the new covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-144/
- Spurgeon: under the Old Testament, Israel had earthly rewards for obedience. The second half of the verse corrects the first: the heart of happiness is being right with God. Those without earthly wealth still have "the gold of heaven." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps144.php
- Matthew Henry reads the verse as David correcting himself: the people whose God is the LORD are happier still, even without much of this world's goods. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_144.cfm
- Constable: those who look to the LORD for deliverance will enjoy his blessing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-144.html
- Seedbed (Wesleyan) says the psalm's ending looks forward to the peace and plenty that will come when God "comes down," not just back to David's day. https://seedbed.com/god-coming-down-to-repair-the-world-psalm-144/
- Kingcomments sees Solomon's reign as a foretaste of these blessings for a future remnant of Israel under Christ. Belonging to the LORD is the greater blessing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/psalms/144.htm

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ
I found only one clear disagreement that follows tradition lines.
- **v. 9, instruments in worship:** Spurgeon (Baptist) says instruments are acceptable when they serve the singing. He won't condemn churches that use them, but he prefers simple unaccompanied praise as closer to the spirit of the gospel than "pomp of organs." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps144.php

  Augustine reads the ten-stringed harp symbolically, as the Ten Commandments. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801144.htm

  I found no Lutheran, Methodist or Pentecostal source arguing the other side on this verse.

The other differences I found are between individual writers, not traditions:
- the two Pulpit sermon writers on v. 1 and war (above);
- earthly rewards versus spiritual happiness in v. 15. Spurgeon (Baptist) and Henry (Presbyterian) actually agree that the second half of the verse ranks above the first.

Gill (Baptist and Calvinist) and Wesley and Clarke (Methodist) agree in substance on every verse where my extracts had both.

## 3. Other views
- **Critical scholarship (Ellicott):** vv. 1–11 are a late patchwork mostly from Psalm 18, and vv. 12–15 are an unrelated older fragment. Spurgeon and Constable reject or soften this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-144.html
- **v. 12 – whose sons?** The ancient Greek and Latin translations read "whose sons are like plants." Gill reports that some therefore take vv. 12–14 as the empty boasts of the wicked foreigners, though he reads them as David's prayer for his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/144.htm

  A commentary quoted on Biblehub calls the "enemies" reading improbable. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/144-14.htm

  Coffman reports Rawlinson's view that some later critics read vv. 12–14 in the present tense, as a description of Israel's actual condition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/144-13.html
- **Catholic / patristic (Augustine):** Augustine follows the Greek "whose sons." He says vv. 12ff. describe the earthly happiness of the "strangers," which Christians should not envy. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801144.htm

  He reads the whole psalm as spoken by Christ and his Body, the Church. In the title he finds David against Goliath, a picture of Christ defeating the devil with his own weapons. In v. 1 the "fingers" are the Spirit's different gifts working together. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801144.htm

  Note: Augustine's sermon uses the old Greek and Latin numbering (Psalm 143), but the New Advent page is titled Psalm 144.
